title: Clockwise Order via Relabeling
content: IsCWOrder is defined as IsCCWOrder with points z₂ and z₄ swapped: z₁, z₄, z₃, z₂ go counterclockwise iff z₁, z₂, z₃, z₄ go clockwise. This definitional reduction is elegant — it means every theorem about CCW order can be applied to CW order by relabeling. The FourDistinct structure bundles all six pairwise distinctness conditions (C(4,2) = 6 pairs), making hypotheses ergonomic to pass around and providing the lemma FourDistinct.reverse which converts distinctness under the relabeling z₁z₂z₃z₄ → z₁z₄z₃z₂.
mathContext: $\text{IsCWOrder}(z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4) := \text{IsCCWOrder}(z_1,z_4,z_3,z_2)$. Equivalently, as one traverses $z_1 \to z_2 \to z_3 \to z_4$ on the unit circle, the angles decrease (mod $2\pi$).

title: Triangle Inequality Equality Case → Positive Proportionality
content: This is the algebraic heart of the converse. The Ptolemy equality ‖z₁-z₃‖·‖z₂-z₄‖ = ‖z₁-z₂‖·‖z₃-z₄‖ + ‖z₂-z₃‖·‖z₁-z₄‖ is rewritten as ‖a+b‖ = ‖a‖ + ‖b‖ using the algebraic identity (z₁-z₂)(z₃-z₄) + (z₂-z₃)(z₁-z₄) = (z₁-z₃)(z₂-z₄). In a strictly convex normed space (which ℂ is as a real inner product space), equality in the triangle inequality forces the two summands to lie on the same ray: SameRay ℝ a b. Since both factors are nonzero (from FourDistinct), this gives a positive real scalar t with t•a = b. The key step (ptolemy_equality_implies_proportional) was developed in PtolemysComplexProofOQ01.
mathContext: Using the algebraic identity $(z_1-z_2)(z_3-z_4) + (z_2-z_3)(z_1-z_4) = (z_1-z_3)(z_2-z_4)$, Ptolemy equality becomes $\|a+b\| = \|a\| + \|b\|$. In a strictly convex space, this implies $\exists t > 0$: $t \cdot (z_1-z_2)(z_3-z_4) = (z_2-z_3)(z_1-z_4)$.

title: Angular Case Analysis: The Remaining Axiom
content: This axiom captures the geometric step: given that the cross-ratio (z₁-z₂)(z₃-z₄)/((z₂-z₃)(z₁-z₄)) is a positive real number, the four unit-circle points must be in CCW or CW order. The mathematical proof uses the exp difference factorization: zᵢ - zⱼ = 2i·sin((θᵢ-θⱼ)/2)·exp(i(θᵢ+θⱼ)/2). The four exponential phase factors E₁₂, E₃₄, E₂₃, E₁₄ all equal exp(i(θ₁+θ₂+θ₃+θ₄)/2) when multiplied in pairs, so they cancel. The (2i)² factors also cancel, leaving t·sin((θ₁-θ₂)/2)·sin((θ₃-θ₄)/2) = sin((θ₂-θ₃)/2)·sin((θ₁-θ₄)/2). With t > 0, both products must have the same sign. Among all possible orderings of four distinct points on a circle, only CCW and CW orderings give same-sign sine products on both sides.
mathContext: With $z_j = e^{i\theta_j}$: $z_i - z_j = 2i \sin\!\tfrac{\theta_i-\theta_j}{2} \cdot e^{i(\theta_i+\theta_j)/2}$. Cross-ratio condition $\Rightarrow$ $t \cdot s_{12} s_{34} = s_{23} s_{14}$ where $s_{ij} = \sin\!\tfrac{\theta_i - \theta_j}{2}$. Same-sign condition identifies exactly the CCW and CW orderings.

title: Main Theorem: Two-Step Composition
content: The main theorem ptolemy_equality_implies_ccw_or_cw is a clean two-line proof: first apply ptolemy_eq_implies_pos_prop to extract the positive proportionality constant t, then apply positive_ratio_implies_cyclic_order to conclude CCW or CW order. The proof is essentially a pipeline through two independently established lemmas. This modular decomposition — separating the algebraic/normed-space step from the trigonometric/cyclic-order step — makes the proof architecture clear and the remaining axiom tightly scoped.
mathContext: Proof chain: Ptolemy equality $\xrightarrow{\text{strict convexity}}$ $\exists t>0: t \cdot (z_1-z_2)(z_3-z_4) = (z_2-z_3)(z_1-z_4)$ $\xrightarrow{\text{sign analysis}}$ CCW $\vee$ CW.

title: CW Direction via Relabeling and Norm Symmetry
content: Proving Ptolemy equality for CW order is handled by relabeling: IsCWOrder(z₁,z₂,z₃,z₄) is by definition IsCCWOrder(z₁,z₄,z₃,z₂), so the forward theorem applies to the permuted sequence (z₁,z₄,z₃,z₂). The result after applying ptolemy_equality_for_unit_circle_ccw is: ‖z₁-z₃‖·‖z₄-z₂‖ = ‖z₁-z₄‖·‖z₃-z₂‖ + ‖z₄-z₃‖·‖z₁-z₂‖. Three applications of norm_sub_rev (‖a-b‖ = ‖b-a‖) bring the norms to canonical form, and linarith closes the goal using multiplication commutativity. The complete biconditional theorem ptolemy_equality_iff_ccw_or_cw then follows by rintro case split.
mathContext: The Ptolemy equality is symmetric in the ordering of norms: $\|a-b\| = \|b-a\|$ and $\|a\|\cdot\|b\| = \|b\|\cdot\|a\|$ allow converting between the permuted form and the canonical form, closing the CW direction without new mathematical content.

title: Numerical Sanity Check: Square on Unit Circle
content: The numerical example verifies Ptolemy equality for the CW sequence 1, -i, -1, i (the four vertices of a square inscribed in the unit circle, traversed clockwise). The computation: ‖1-(-1)‖·‖(-i)-i‖ = 2·2 = 4, and ‖1-(-i)‖·‖(-1)-i‖ + ‖(-i)-(-1)‖·‖1-i‖ = √2·√2 + √2·√2 = 4. The proof uses norm_num to verify the complex arithmetic. This serves as a concrete sanity check that the CW theorem gives the right answer for a familiar example — the diagonals of a square equal the sum of products of opposite sides, which is just the statement that 2·2 = 2.
mathContext: For the unit square: $|1-(-1)| \cdot |{-i}-i| = 2 \cdot 2 = 4$ and $|1-(-i)| \cdot |{-1}-i| + |{-i}-(-1)| \cdot |1-i| = \sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2} = 4$. A square satisfies Ptolemy equality because its diagonals have length $\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2} = 2$ times each side.
